title: Thomson Reuters Opens Early Access to the 'Next Generation' of CoCounsel Legal, Saying Beta Users 'F#@%ing Loved' the Product
author: Robert Ambrogi

dom.t: Legal agents: Connected matter work retains review

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts the need for selective, human-centred deployment and materially extends it with concrete product designs: authority-grounded drafting with citation checking, matter-specific continuity, and a layer for encoding lawyers’ expertise across workflows. Its support is primarily a vendor roadmap and attributed beta feedback, not independent evidence of reliability or organisational value.
qs: - **Brief Builder**, an agentic drafting tool for briefs and motions grounded in Westlaw and Practical Law authority, with citation checking and issue spotting built in.

- **Firm and organizational intelligence**, described as a skill-authoring layer that lets lawyers encode their own expertise into the system so it is applied consistently across matters and across a team.

st.t: Legal agents: Connected matter work retains review
st.an: The source directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition: CoCounsel is shifting from discrete assistance to connected, multistep matter work while keeping lawyers in the review loop. It also supports the cluster’s evidentiary caution by presenting usefulness through attributed beta testimonials and company claims rather than comparative performance measurements.
qs: A user describes a matter in plain language; the system drafts a plan, works through the legal issues, pulls from the user's own precedents as well as from Westlaw and Practical Law, drafts with citations, and adapts as new information surfaces.

Analogizing it to a senior associate, Colbert and Ashraf said that beta testers stopped comparing CoCounsel Legal to other AI tools and began comparing it to a skilled junior lawyer whose work comes back "verifiable, ready for review, and open to iteration."  ## They 'F#@%ing Loved' the Product  Launch materials provided by Thomson Reuters are unusually emphatic, even by the standards of product announcements.

kp.k: Early access precedes planned international rollout
kp.d: Ambrogi reports that Thomson Reuters rebuilt CoCounsel Legal on Anthropic's Claude Agent SDK. According to the company, all U.S. CoCounsel Legal customers can switch between the new and current versions during early access beginning this week. U.S. general availability is planned for August 2026, followed by Canada, the U.K., and Australia; pricing was not specified.
qs: Starting this week, every CoCounsel Legal customer in the United States will see a toggle in the product allowing them to switch into the new experience and back to the current version at will, the company says.
Thomson Reuters says full general availability is planned for August 2026 in the U.S., followed by rollouts in Canada, the U.K., and Australia.
The company did not specify pricing.

kp.k: Agentic workflows replace discrete task-based skills
kp.d: Thomson Reuters product co-heads Emily Colbert and Rawia Ashraf describe a shift from user-selected skills, structured workflows, and detailed prompts toward a system that plans and executes work from a plain-language matter description. The claimed workflow combines users' precedents with Westlaw and Practical Law, produces cited drafts, and adapts to new information to deliver an iterative work product rather than separate answers.
qs: A user selected a skill, defined a workflow, or wrote a detailed prompt, and results came back task by task.

A user describes a matter in plain language; the system drafts a plan, works through the legal issues, pulls from the user's own precedents as well as from Westlaw and Practical Law, drafts with citations, and adapts as new information surfaces.
The result, Thomson Reuters says, is a single, iterable work product rather than a series of piecemeal answers.

kp.d: Colbert and Ashraf analogize the product to a senior associate and report that beta testers compared it to a skilled junior lawyer rather than other AI tools. Their framing emphasizes work available for verification, review, and iteration, rather than output presented as requiring no lawyer review.
qs: Analogizing it to a senior associate, Colbert and Ashraf said that beta testers stopped comparing CoCounsel Legal to other AI tools and began comparing it to a skilled junior lawyer whose work comes back "verifiable, ready for review, and open to iteration."

kp.k: Vendor-carried testimonials suggest broader everyday adoption
kp.d: Launch materials from Colbert and Ashraf report testers beginning nearly every project in the new experience. Customer testimonials carried by Thomson Reuters include Dan Block describing it as an early choice for work, Andrew Medeiros reporting adoption across seniority levels and practice areas, and Amber Simon reporting unsolicited identification of an anti-assignment issue and a 10/10 experience rating. These are attributed beta-user accounts, not measured productivity findings.
qs: Instead, they received unsolicited praise, including from testers who reported that they had begun starting nearly every project in the new experience rather than reserving it for specific tasks.
Andrew Medeiros, managing director of innovation at Troutman Pepper Locke, points to adoption "from associates to partners across every practice area."
Amber Simon, an attorney at Polsinelli, says the tool flagged an anti-assignment issue she had not yet asked about and rates the experience a "10/10."

kp.k: Reported applications extend beyond litigation and research
kp.d: Thomson Reuters reports that transactional and specialist beta users, including employee-benefits attorneys, found applications they had assumed unavailable in a product historically strongest in litigation and research. This is a company account of testers' experiences rather than a quantified comparison across practice areas.
qs: Thomson Reuters also says the breadth of the product surprised testers, with transactional and specialist attorneys — including in areas such as employee benefits — reporting use cases they had assumed were out of reach for a tool historically strongest in litigation and research.

kp.k: Matter persistence and encoded expertise expand workflow scope
kp.d: The company describes three capabilities still rolling out: Workspaces, already live and continuing to develop, preserves matter documents, precedents, and positions across sessions and colleagues; Brief Builder provides agentic brief and motion drafting with citation checking and issue spotting; and a skill-authoring layer is intended to apply lawyers' encoded expertise consistently across matters and teams.
qs: **Workspaces**, a dedicated environment for each matter that carries a user's documents, precedents, and prior positions across sessions and colleagues. The company says Workspaces is live today and will continue to develop.
**Brief Builder**, an agentic drafting tool for briefs and motions grounded in Westlaw and Practical Law authority, with citation checking and issue spotting built in.

**Firm and organizational intelligence**, described as a skill-authoring layer that lets lawyers encode their own expertise into the system so it is applied consistently across matters and across a team.

kp.d: Colbert, Ashraf, and CTO Joel Hron promote the company's concept of fiduciary-grade AI for work subject to regulatory oversight and duties of care. Thomson Reuters says this entails authoritative grounding from the start of reasoning, linked citations, inspectable reasoning, and no use of confidential data to train third-party models. Hron argues that professionals' ability to verify and stand behind systems will define professional AI's future, rather than answer speed alone.
qs: The company says the standard means outputs are grounded in authoritative content from the first step of reasoning rather than checked against sources afterward, that every citation is traceable to a linked source, that the reasoning process is inspectable, and that confidential data is not used to train third-party models.
"The future of professional AI will not be defined only by who can generate the fastest answer," Hron wrote. "It will be defined by which systems professionals can verify, trust, and stand behind."

kp.k: Platform integrations support an agentic operating-system strategy
kp.d: Hron positions CoCounsel as an emerging agentic operating system accessible within existing professional tools rather than solely as a standalone destination. He reports engagement with Google, Microsoft, OpenAI, AWS, and Anthropic on APIs, connectors, and Model Context Protocol access. The company announces planned connections to document, practice, and enterprise platforms and says its recently announced Anthropic MCP integration enables access from Claude without switching platforms.
qs: Hron's article builds on that concept to describe a product strategy, positioning CoCounsel as an emerging "agentic operating system" for the professions Thomson Reuters serves — a system meant to be available not only as a destination but across the tools, models, and platforms where customers already work.
He says the company is engaging with Google, Microsoft, OpenAI, AWS, and Anthropic, among others, to make CoCounsel reachable through APIs, connectors, and the Model Context Protocol.

With regard to integrations, the company says CoCounsel Legal will connect to Microsoft 365, HighQ, iManage, NetDocuments, SharePoint, Icertis, DeepJudge, Supio, and Smokeball, and that its recently announced MCP integration with Anthropic lets lawyers working in Claude reach CoCounsel Legal without switching platforms.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Thomson Reuters presents the rebuilt CoCounsel Legal as an agent that produces an integrated, revisable legal work product rather than isolated task answers.
pts.d: Ambrogi reports claims by Thomson Reuters and its legal product co-heads Emily Colbert and Rawia Ashraf that lawyers can describe a matter in plain language rather than select discrete skills or construct detailed workflows. The system then plans, works through issues, draws on firm precedents and legal sources, and drafts with citations. Their comparisons to a senior associate and a skilled junior lawyer describe reviewable assistance, not autonomous substitution for a lawyer.

pts.k: Colbert and Ashraf claim the new version is becoming a starting point for projects, with use extending beyond litigation and research.
pts.d: Their launch materials report that some beta testers began nearly every project in the new experience. Thomson Reuters also reports previously unexpected uses among transactional and specialist attorneys, including employee benefits practitioners. These are claims about beta-user experience and expanding applicability, not demonstrated profession-wide adoption.

pts.k: Thomson Reuters says additional capabilities will support persistent matter context, agentic brief drafting, and consistent application of organizational expertise.
pts.d: Workspaces is intended to retain documents, precedents, and prior positions across sessions and colleagues. Brief Builder is described as drafting briefs and motions with citation checking and issue spotting. A skill-authoring layer is intended to let lawyers encode expertise for reuse across matters and teams. Workspaces is reported as already live; the other capabilities are described as still rolling out.

pts.k: Thomson Reuters claims its approach supports professional verification, confidentiality, and accountability; CTO Joel Hron predicts these qualities will define professional AI's future.
pts.d: The company uses the term 'fiduciary-grade AI' for systems intended for regulated work involving duties of care. It claims authoritative grounding from the beginning of reasoning, linked citations, inspectable reasoning, and protection against third-party model training on confidential data. Hron's broader prediction emphasizes professionals' ability to verify and stand behind outputs rather than answer speed alone. The article presents this as a company standard and strategy, not as an independently certified status.

pts.k: Hron positions CoCounsel as an emerging professional operating system accessible within existing work platforms.
pts.d: Hron describes a strategy of making CoCounsel available through APIs, connectors, and the Model Context Protocol rather than solely as a standalone destination. Thomson Reuters identifies planned connections to document, productivity, and legal-work platforms and says its Anthropic MCP integration enables lawyers using Claude to reach CoCounsel Legal without switching platforms.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence offered consists of company descriptions, executive statements, and company-supplied beta-user testimonials.
pts.d: Ambrogi draws on a LinkedIn Live event, launch materials by Colbert and Ashraf, and a companion article by Hron. Reported testimonials concern workflow adoption, use across seniority levels and practice areas, and an instance of unsolicited issue spotting. These testimonials support the company's account of user experience; the article supplies no quantitative benchmark, controlled comparison, measured accuracy rate, or measured productivity gain. The roadmap and operating-system vision are supported by company announcements rather than demonstrated market outcomes.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Early access begins in the week of the article's 22 June 2026 publication; U.S. general availability is planned for August 2026, with further geographic and feature rollouts to follow.
pts.d: The early-access offer applies to existing U.S. CoCounsel Legal customers, who can switch between old and new versions. Canada, the U.K., and Australia are named as subsequent rollout markets without dates. Workspaces is described as live and developing, while Brief Builder and organizational intelligence are still rolling out without individual launch dates. Hron's wider professional-AI prediction has no specified horizon. Pricing is not specified, and the lawyer analogy explicitly retains human review.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The immediate affected users are CoCounsel Legal customers and legal teams, with claimed benefits across seniority levels, practice areas, and existing software environments.
pts.d: The article describes changes to lawyers' matter planning, research, drafting, issue spotting, and review. Company-reported experience includes associates and partners, litigation and research users, and transactional and specialist attorneys. Persistent matter context and encoded expertise are intended to benefit colleagues and teams. Access initially concerns U.S. customers and subsequently the named international markets. The article does not make concrete claims about job losses, staffing ratios, legal fees, client savings, or access to justice.
